How to read today's slides

Every concept follows the same five steps

Idea. A small example on the chain, with a picture or an animation. You see the method work before it has a name.
Definition and theorem. The precise statement, with a proof you can follow line by line.
Check. The statement applied to the chain, with exact numbers.
In today's machine learning. Where the same idea runs in current systems, with the paper.
Connection. What the concept cannot do yet: the next question, which the next concept answers.

The rail at the bottom of every slide shows which of the eight concepts we are in.

Only an average is known, and many distributions fit it

  • X∈{0,1,2}X\in\{0,1,2\}X∈{0,1,2}; we know only E[X]=0.5\mathbb E[X]=0.5E[X]=0.5.

Which distribution should we believe?
Answer. Something in between: the most spread-out distribution with mean 0.5. Week 3 measured spread by entropy.

U(T)=EpT[E]=∑xE(x) pT(x)=∑xE(x) e−E(x)/T∑xe−E(x)/T.U(T)=\mathbb E_{p_T}[E]=\sum_xE(x)\,p_T(x)=\frac{\sum_xE(x)\,e^{-E(x)/T}}{\sum_xe^{-E(x)/T}}.U(T)=EpT​​[E]=x∑​E(x)pT​(x)=∑x​e−E(x)/T∑x​E(x)e−E(x)/T​.

U(T)=0⋅1+1⋅r+2⋅r21+r+r2=r+2r21+r+r2.U(T)=\frac{0\cdot1+1\cdot r+2\cdot r^2}{1+r+r^2}=\frac{r+2r^2}{1+r+r^2}.U(T)=1+r+r20⋅1+1⋅r+2⋅r2​=1+r+r2r+2r2​.
U(T)=0.5  ⟺  r+2r2=0.5 (1+r+r2)  ⟺  3r2+r−1=0  ⟺  r=13−16=0.4343.U(T)=0.5\iff r+2r^2=0.5\,(1+r+r^2)\iff 3r^2+r-1=0\iff r=\tfrac{\sqrt{13}-1}{6}=0.4343.U(T)=0.5⟺r+2r2=0.5(1+r+r2)⟺3r2+r−1=0⟺r=613​−1​=0.4343.

1 · Maximum entropy · Theorem

At a fixed average energy, the Boltzmann distribution has the largest entropy

Theorem 1. Fix an energy EEE and a temperature TTT. Let pTp_TpT​ be the Boltzmann distribution
pT(x)=e−E(x)/TZT,ZT=∑xe−E(x)/T,p_T(x)=\frac{e^{-E(x)/T}}{Z_T},\qquad Z_T=\sum_xe^{-E(x)/T},pT​(x)=ZT​e−E(x)/T​,ZT​=x∑​e−E(x)/T,
and U=EpT[E]U=\mathbb E_{p_T}[E]U=EpT​​[E] its average energy. Every qqq with Eq[E]=U\mathbb E_q[E]=UEq​[E]=U has H(q)≤H(pT)H(q)\le H(p_T)H(q)≤H(pT​), with equality only for q=pTq=p_Tq=pT​.
Proof. Average Fact 1 under qqq, not under pTp_TpT​. Since qqq has the same mean energy UUU:
H(q,pT)=−∑xq(x)ln⁡pT(x)=∑xq(x)(E(x)T+ln⁡ZT)=UT+ln⁡ZT=H(pT)(Fact 2).H(q,p_T)=-\sum_xq(x)\ln p_T(x)=\sum_x q(x)\Big(\frac{E(x)}{T}+\ln Z_T\Big)=\frac{U}{T}+\ln Z_T=H(p_T)\quad\text{(Fact 2)}.H(q,pT​)=−x∑​q(x)lnpT​(x)=x∑​q(x)(TE(x)​+lnZT​)=TU​+lnZT​=H(pT​)(Fact 2).
H(pT)−H(q)=H(q,pT)−H(q)=DKL(q ∥ pT) ≥ 0(Fact 3).■H(p_T)-H(q)=H(q,p_T)-H(q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\,\|\,p_T)\ \ge\ 0\quad\text{(Fact 3)}.\qquad\blacksquareH(pT​)−H(q)=H(q,pT​)−H(q)=DKL​(q∥pT​) ≥ 0(Fact 3).■

1 · Maximum entropy · Example

Pair averages cannot see a rule that involves three variables

  • Week 3's XOR: X,YX,YX,Y fair coins, W=X⊕YW=X\oplus YW=X⊕Y. Only four states occur, xyw=000,011,101,110xyw=000,011,101,110xyw=000,011,101,110, each 14\tfrac1441​.
  • One variable at a time: each of X,Y,WX,Y,WX,Y,W is 1 in two of the four states, so each is 1 with probability 12\tfrac1221​.
  • Two at a time: each pair, e.g. (X,W)(X,W)(X,W), takes the values 00, 01, 11, 10 once each, so each combination has probability 14\tfrac1441​.
  • Three independent fair coins give exactly the same one- and two-variable statistics. Only all three together reveal W=X⊕YW=X\oplus YW=X⊕Y.
  • So maximum entropy with these constraints returns three independent coins, uniform on all 8 states. The four impossible states get 18\tfrac1881​ each.
1 · Maximum entropy · Activity

Which local function restores the missing rule?

Pair factors cannot express W=X⊕YW=X\oplus YW=X⊕Y. What can?
Answer. One square joined to all three circles: f(x,y,w)=1f(x,y,w)=1f(x,y,w)=1 if w=x⊕yw=x\oplus yw=x⊕y, else 0. Its feature sxsysws_xs_ys_wsx​sy​sw​ has data average −1-1−1.
  • With this factor the model keeps exactly the four possible states: H=ln⁡4H=\ln4H=ln4.
  • Those states, 000, 011, 101, 110, each contain an even number of ones. So the factor is a parity check: 1 for an even count, 0 for an odd count.
  • The same check works for more bits. On four bits it keeps the 8 of 16 states with an even count, such as 0000, 0011, 1111, and removes the other 8.
1 · Maximum entropy · Note

Maximum entropy is a modeling principle, not a guarantee about the world

Fitting pθp_\thetapθ​ to measured averages makes three different claims:

Claim 1. Its averages equal the measured ones. Provable: this is how θ\thetaθ is chosen.
Claim 2. Among all distributions with those averages, it has the largest entropy. Provable: Theorem 2.
Claim 3. It matches the real system. Not provable. XOR satisfies Claims 1 and 2 and still puts 12\tfrac1221​ on impossible states.

So test a fitted model on a property you did not use to fit it. An omitted relationship stays omitted, however exact the arithmetic.

The softmax classifier is the maximum-entropy model

  • Features ϕk(x,y)\phi_k(x,y)ϕk​(x,y) of an input xxx and a label yyy.
  • Theorem 2 applied to each input: the maximum-entropy model with those averages is a softmax.
  • Text classifiers were built this way in the 1990s (Berger, Della Pietra and Della Pietra, 1996).
  • A language model's output layer is the same form: logits zyz_yzy​, probabilities ezy/∑y′ezy′e^{z_y}/\sum_{y'}e^{z_{y'}}ezy​/∑y′​ezy′​ over the vocabulary.
  • The denominator is a small sum here, one term per token. It becomes impossible when yyy is a whole response or an image.

A. L. Berger, S. A. Della Pietra, V. J. Della Pietra. A maximum entropy approach to natural language processing. Computational Linguistics 22(1), 39–71, 1996.

Does a matching θ\thetaθ exist, and is it unique?

Existence. The argument above needs a θ\thetaθ whose averages equal mmm. For an extreme average such as E[s1]=1\mathbb E[s_1]=1E[s1​]=1, no finite θ\thetaθ works (next slides).
Uniqueness and linear dependence. The features are linearly dependent if some v≠0v\ne0v=0 makes ∑kvkϕk(x)\sum_kv_k\phi_k(x)∑k​vk​ϕk​(x) the same constant for every xxx. Then Var⁡(∑kvkϕk)=0\operatorname{Var}(\sum_kv_k\phi_k)=0Var(∑k​vk​ϕk​)=0: the log-likelihood is flat along vvv, and many θ\thetaθ fit equally well.
Example: one binary xxx with ϕ1=x\phi_1=xϕ1​=x, ϕ2=1−x\phi_2=1-xϕ2​=1−x. Since ϕ1+ϕ2=1\phi_1+\phi_2=1ϕ1​+ϕ2​=1, the parameters θ\thetaθ and θ+t(1,1)\theta+t(1,1)θ+t(1,1) multiply every weight by the same ete^tet, which cancels in ZZZ: the same model.

With linearly independent features, θ\thetaθ is unique. Either way, the fitted distribution is unique (Theorem 2); only its parameters can be redundant.

Next-token training: the gradient of one record

Fix one context ccc, say “The cat sat on the”. The network reads ccc and outputs one real number per vocabulary token kkk, its logit zkz_kzk​. (In a transformer, zk=wk⋅hcz_k=w_k\cdot h_czk​=wk​⋅hc​: the final hidden state hch_chc​ times token kkk's output vector wkw_kwk​.) The softmax turns logits into probabilities:

pθ(k)=ezk∑jezj: the exponential family with ϕk=1[next token=k] and knob θk=zk.p_\theta(k)=\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_je^{z_j}}:\ \text{the exponential family with }\phi_k=\mathbb 1[\text{next token}=k]\text{ and knob }\theta_k=z_k.pθ​(k)=∑j​ezj​ezk​​: the exponential family with ϕk​=1[next token=k] and knob θk​=zk​.

One record: context ccc, then token yyy. Its loss is the surprise of yyy:

−ln⁡pθ(y)=−zy+ln⁡∑jezj,∂(−ln⁡pθ(y))∂zk=−1[k=y]+ezk∑jezj=pθ(k)−1[k=y].\begin{aligned}-\ln p_\theta(y)&=-z_y+\ln\sum_je^{z_j},\\ \frac{\partial\big(-\ln p_\theta(y)\big)}{\partial z_k}&=-\mathbb 1[k=y]+\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_je^{z_j}}=p_\theta(k)-\mathbb 1[k=y].\end{aligned}−lnpθ​(y)∂zk​∂(−lnpθ​(y))​​=−zy​+lnj∑​ezj​,=−1[k=y]+∑j​ezj​ezk​​=pθ​(k)−1[k=y].​

One record alone is a poor target: 1[k=y]\mathbb 1[k=y]1[k=y] is 0 or 1, extreme (Warning 1). Next: average over the corpus.

2 · Moment matching · In today's machine learning

Over the corpus, next-token training is moment matching

  • The context ccc occurs nnn times in the corpus, followed by tokens y(1),…,y(n)y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(n)}y(1),…,y(n).
  • Average the one-record gradient over them: 1n∑i=1n(pθ(k)−1[y(i)=k])=pθ(k)−f(k),\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(p_\theta(k)-\mathbb 1[y^{(i)}=k]\big)=p_\theta(k)-f(k),n1​i=1∑n​(pθ​(k)−1[y(i)=k])=pθ​(k)−f(k), where f(k)f(k)f(k) is the fraction of those records whose next token is kkk: the data average of ϕk\phi_kϕk​.
  • Zero gradient   ⟺  pθ(k)=f(k)\iff p_\theta(k)=f(k)⟺pθ​(k)=f(k): the model's probabilities match the corpus frequencies.
  • This is Theorem 4: the log-likelihood gradient is data average minus model average, mk−Eθ[ϕk];m_k-\mathbb E_\theta[\phi_k];mk​−Eθ​[ϕk​]; here mk=f(k)m_k=f(k)mk​=f(k) and Eθ[ϕk]=pθ(k).\mathbb E_\theta[\phi_k]=p_\theta(k).Eθ​[ϕk​]=pθ​(k). The loss is minus the log-likelihood, so its gradient is pθ(k)−f(k).p_\theta(k)-f(k).pθ​(k)−f(k).
2 · Moment matching · In today's machine learning

Boltzmann machines learn by data correlation minus model correlation

Jij ← Jij+η (⟨sisj⟩data−⟨sisj⟩model)⏟ΔJij, the change in one step(Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski, 1985)J_{ij}\ \leftarrow\ J_{ij}+\underbrace{\eta\,\big(\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\text{data}}-\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\text{model}}\big)}_{\Delta J_{ij},\ \text{the change in one step}}\qquad\text{(Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski, 1985)}Jij​ ← Jij​+ΔJij​, the change in one stepη(⟨si​sj​⟩data​−⟨si​sj​⟩model​)​​(Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski, 1985)
  • ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle⟨⋅⟩ means an average: ⟨sisj⟩data\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\text{data}}⟨si​sj​⟩data​ over the training examples, ⟨sisj⟩model=Eθ[sisj]\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\text{model}}=\mathbb E_\theta[s_is_j]⟨si​sj​⟩model​=Eθ​[si​sj​]. This is our fitting rule for the knob JijJ_{ij}Jij​ (Theorem 4).
  • Data term: cheap. Model term: a sum over all 2n2^n2n spin states, estimated by running the Boltzmann machine, that is, by sampling.
  • Contrastive divergence starts that sampler at the data and runs only a few steps (Hinton, 2002). Energy-based image models do the same (Du and Mordatch, 2019).

Ackley, Hinton, Sejnowski, Cognitive Science 1985; Hinton, Neural Computation 2002; Du, Mordatch, NeurIPS 2019. Full references at the end.

How one independent draw from ppp is made on our chain

Lay the eight weights side by side on [0,78)[0,78)[0,78). A uniform random uuu lands in one segment, so state xxx is hit with probability g(x)/78=p(x)g(x)/78=p(x)g(x)/78=p(x). Above: u=50u=50u=50 lands in 101.

cum = [12, 16, 17, 21, 45, 53, 58, 78]      # running totals of g over 000, 001, ..., 111

x = states[bisect.bisect_right(cum, u)]     # the state whose segment contains u

Each draw uses fresh randomness, so the draws are independent. But the recipe needs the total Z=78Z=78Z=78: fine for 8 states, impossible for 210242^{1024}21024.

3 · Monte Carlo · Definition and theorem

Monte Carlo is unbiased, and its error shrinks like 1/N1/\sqrt N1/N​

Definition (Monte Carlo estimate). Independent draws x(1),…,x(N)x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(N)}x(1),…,x(N) from ppp:
μ^N=1N∑t=1Ng(x(t)) ≈ μ=Ep[g]=∑xp(x) g(x).\hat\mu_N=\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^Ng\big(x^{(t)}\big)\ \approx\ \mu=\mathbb E_p[g]=\sum_xp(x)\,g(x).μ^​N​=N1​t=1∑N​g(x(t)) ≈ μ=Ep​[g]=x∑​p(x)g(x).
Theorem 5. E[μ^N]=μ\mathbb E[\hat\mu_N]=\muE[μ^​N​]=μ (unbiased) and Var⁡(μ^N)=σ2/N\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_N)=\sigma^2/NVar(μ^​N​)=σ2/N, where σ2=Var⁡p(g)=Ep[(g(X)−μ)2]\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}_p(g)=\mathbb E_p\big[(g(X)-\mu)^2\big]σ2=Varp​(g)=Ep​[(g(X)−μ)2] is the variance of one draw.
Proof. Expectation is linear: E[μ^N]=1N∑tE[g(x(t))]=1N⋅Nμ\mathbb E[\hat\mu_N]=\frac1N\sum_t\mathbb E[g(x^{(t)})]=\frac1N\cdot N\muE[μ^​N​]=N1​∑t​E[g(x(t))]=N1​⋅Nμ. The draws are independent, so their variances add: Var⁡(μ^N)=1N2⋅Nσ2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_N)=\frac1{N^2}\cdot N\sigma^2Var(μ^​N​)=N21​⋅Nσ2. ■\blacksquare■
Definition (standard error). SE=Var⁡(μ^N)=σ/N\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_N)}=\sigma/\sqrt NSE=Var(μ^​N​)​=σ/N​. Since E[μ^N]=μ\mathbb E[\hat\mu_N]=\muE[μ^​N​]=μ, it equals the root-mean-square error E[(μ^N−μ)2]\sqrt{\mathbb E[(\hat\mu_N-\mu)^2]}E[(μ^​N​−μ)2]​: the typical distance of the estimate from μ\muμ.

The proof uses only linearity and independence, no central limit theorem. A. B. Owen. Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples. 2013, Chapter 2.

4 · Markov chains · Definition

A Markov chain chooses the next state by looking only at the current one

Definition (Markov chain). States X0,X1,X2,…X_0,X_1,X_2,\dotsX0​,X1​,X2​,… with a transition matrix
P(x,x′)=Pr⁡(Xt+1=x′∣Xt=x),P(x,x′)≥0,∑x′P(x,x′)=1 (each row).P(x,x')=\Pr(X_{t+1}=x'\mid X_t=x),\qquad P(x,x')\ge0,\qquad \sum_{x'}P(x,x')=1\ \text{(each row)}.P(x,x′)=Pr(Xt+1​=x′∣Xt​=x),P(x,x′)≥0,x′∑​P(x,x′)=1 (each row).
Given the present, the past carries no extra information about the next step.
The fair-coin walk, row of state 000. Pick X1X_1X1​, X2X_2X2​ or X3X_3X3​ with probability 13\tfrac1331​; the coin keeps the current value with probability 12\tfrac1221​:
P(000,000)=12,P(000,100)=P(000,010)=P(000,001)=13⋅12=16.P(000,000)=\tfrac12,\qquad P(000,100)=P(000,010)=P(000,001)=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac16.P(000,000)=21​,P(000,100)=P(000,010)=P(000,001)=31​⋅21​=61​.

Row sum: 12+3⋅16=1\tfrac12+3\cdot\tfrac16=121​+3⋅61​=1. Every row looks the same: stay with 12\tfrac1221​, go to each neighbour with 16\tfrac1661​.

4 · Markov chains · Theorem

From any start the walkers' distribution converges, if the chain is irreducible and aperiodic

Theorem 6 (convergence). A finite chain that is irreducible (every state can reach every other) and aperiodic (not locked into returning only at multiples of some period d≥2d\ge2d≥2) has exactly one stationary π\piπ, and μt→π\mu_t\to\piμt​→π from every start.
  • Fair coin: irreducible (flips connect the cube) and aperiodic (it can stay put). Its distance falls to 0.
  • Always flip: the walkers alternate between the 4 states with an odd number of ones and the 4 with an even number, so half of them are always misplaced: distance ≥0.5\ge0.5≥0.5 (period 2).
4 · Markov chains · Theorem

One walker followed for a long time is as good as many walkers

Theorem 7 (ergodic theorem). For an irreducible finite chain with stationary π\piπ, from any start, with probability 1,
1N∑t=1Ng(Xt) ⟶ Eπ[g]as N→∞.\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^Ng(X_t)\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_\pi[g]\quad\text{as }N\to\infty.N1​t=1∑N​g(Xt​) ⟶ Eπ​[g]as N→∞.
  • With g=1[X=x]g=\mathbb 1[X=x]g=1[X=x]: the fraction of time at xxx tends to π(x)\pi(x)π(x). Left: one fair-coin walker, π(x)=18\pi(x)=\tfrac18π(x)=81​.
  • One long run replaces independent draws from ppp (which need ZZZ). Price: the steps are correlated, so NNN steps are worth fewer than NNN draws.
  • Plan: build PPP with π=p\pi=pπ=p, run one chain, average along the way.
4 · Markov chains · In today's machine learning

Diffusion models run a Markov chain into its stationary distribution, then back

  • Forward process: a Markov chain that adds noise; here each pixel flips with probability 0.1 per step. On our cube: flip each xix_ixi​ with probability 0.1.
  • Its stationary distribution is pure noise: every pixel a fair coin, as the fair-coin walk ends at 18\tfrac1881​ per state. Images use Gaussian noise, text [MASK] tokens, crystals random atoms (MatterGen).
  • Generation starts from that noise and runs a learned chain backwards. You built the forward chain in Laboratory 2.

Ho, Jain and Abbeel, NeurIPS 2020; Austin et al., NeurIPS 2021; Zeni et al., Nature 2025. Full entries on the reference slides.

5 · Detailed balance · Idea

Count the walkers crossing one edge, and see why the fair-coin walk cannot keep ppp

  • Setup: 624 walkers (8×788\times788×78: whole counts). Count those crossing edge 000–100 in one step: each crosses with 13\tfrac1331​ (it picks X1X_1X1​) × 12\times\,\tfrac12×21​ (the coin changes it) =16=\tfrac16=61​, either way.
  • Spread uniformly (78 at each end): 78/6=1378/6=1378/6=13 cross each way. Balanced: the counts stay.
  • Spread as ppp (624⋅1278=96624\cdot\tfrac{12}{78}=96624⋅7812​=96 at 000, 192 at 100): 16 cross one way, 32 back. Net, 16 per step leave 100: the walkers cannot stay at ppp.
  • The share of walkers making a move is the flow π(x)P(x,x′)\pi(x)P(x,x')π(x)P(x,x′). Question: to keep ppp, how often must a walk cross 000 → 100, compared with back?

Split πP=π\pi P=\piπP=π at a state x′x'x′ into what arrives and what leaves:

5 · Detailed balance · Definition and lemma

Balance every edge, and every state is balanced automatically

Definition (detailed balance). A transition matrix PPP satisfies detailed balance with π\piπ if the two flows on every edge are equal:
π(x) P(x,x′)=π(x′) P(x′,x)for all x,x′.\pi(x)\,P(x,x')=\pi(x')\,P(x',x)\qquad\text{for all }x,x'.π(x)P(x,x′)=π(x′)P(x′,x)for all x,x′.
Lemma 8. Detailed balance implies πP=π\pi P=\piπP=π.
Proof. Sum the definition over xxx:
∑xπ(x)P(x,x′)=∑xπ(x′)P(x′,x)=π(x′)∑xP(x′,x)=π(x′)⋅1.■\sum_x\pi(x)P(x,x')=\sum_x\pi(x')P(x',x)=\pi(x')\sum_xP(x',x)=\pi(x')\cdot1.\qquad\blacksquarex∑​π(x)P(x,x′)=x∑​π(x′)P(x′,x)=π(x′)x∑​P(x′,x)=π(x′)⋅1.■

5 · Detailed balance · Note

Detailed balance is sufficient, not necessary

  • A walk on one face of the cube (4 states): each step, stay with probability 12\tfrac1221​, or move on one way round, 000 → 100 → 110 → 010 → 000.
  • Spread the walkers uniformly over the four states: 14\tfrac1441​ at each. Each state sends half of its 14\tfrac1441​, that is 18\tfrac1881​ of all walkers, and receives 18\tfrac1881​ from the state before it: uniform is stationary.
  • But no edge balances: 000 → 100 carries 18\tfrac1881​, 100 → 000 carries 0.
  • So stationarity does not need detailed balance. We use detailed balance because it is enough, and it can be checked edge by edge.

A chain with detailed balance is also called reversible: on every edge, as many jumps one way as the other.

6 · Metropolis–Hastings · Idea

Propose like the fair coin, then accept just often enough to balance the edge

  • One step of the new walk: propose, that is, pick one of the three variables (probability 13\tfrac1331​) and plan to flip it; then accept the flip, or stay.
  • Edge 000–100, 624 walkers spread as ppp. A walker proposes this edge when it picks X1X_1X1​:
walkerspropose (13\tfrac1331​)acceptcross
000 → 1009632all32
100 → 00019264half32
  • Equal: balanced. Rule: accept a move to a heavier state always; to a lighter one with probability g(lighter)/g(heavier)g(\text{lighter})/g(\text{heavier})g(lighter)/g(heavier), here 12/24=1212/24=\tfrac1212/24=21​:
α(x,x′)=min⁡(1, g(x′)g(x))(Metropolis et al., 1953).\alpha(x,x')=\min\Big(1,\ \frac{g(x')}{g(x)}\Big)\quad\text{(Metropolis et al., 1953).}α(x,x′)=min(1, g(x)g(x′)​)(Metropolis et al., 1953).

6 · Metropolis–Hastings · Idea, step by step

Three proposals on the chain: accepted, rejected, and a move to a lighter state accepted

  • Propose: flip one variable at random.
  • Ratio g(x′)/g(x)g(x')/g(x)g(x′)/g(x): only the flipped variable's factors; no ZZZ.
  • Accept if uuu falls below min⁡(1,ratio)\min(1,\text{ratio})min(1,ratio), where uuu is a fresh random number, uniform on [0,1][0,1][0,1], for each proposal (here 0.47, 0.62, 0.15).
  • Rejected: stay, and count the current state again.
  • Lighter states are sometimes accepted: that is how a walker leaves a peak.
6 · Metropolis–Hastings · Idea, animated

A new acceptance rule, and the walkers settle at ppp

6 · Metropolis–Hastings · Definition

With an uneven proposal, Hastings adds the ratio of proposal probabilities

Definition (Metropolis–Hastings). Target π∝g\pi\propto gπ∝g, proposal q(x′∣x)q(x'\mid x)q(x′∣x). From the current state xxx:
  1. propose x′∼q(⋅∣x)x'\sim q(\cdot\mid x)x′∼q(⋅∣x);
  2. accept with probability α(x,x′)=min⁡{1, g(x′) q(x∣x′)g(x) q(x′∣x)}\displaystyle\alpha(x,x')=\min\Big\{1,\ \frac{g(x')\,q(x\mid x')}{g(x)\,q(x'\mid x)}\Big\}α(x,x′)=min{1, g(x)q(x′∣x)g(x′)q(x∣x′)​};
  3. otherwise stay at xxx, and count xxx again.
  • A symmetric proposal, q(x′∣x)=q(x∣x′)q(x'\mid x)=q(x\mid x')q(x′∣x)=q(x∣x′), gives back the rule of 1953.
  • The target enters only through g(x′)/g(x)g(x')/g(x)g(x′)/g(x): ZZZ is never needed.

N. Metropolis, A. W. Rosenbluth, M. N. Rosenbluth, A. H. Teller, E. Teller. Equation of state calculations by fast computing machines. J. Chem. Phys. 21(6), 1087–1092, 1953. W. K. Hastings. Monte Carlo sampling methods using Markov chains and their applications. Biometrika 57(1), 97–109, 1970.

6 · Metropolis–Hastings · Theorem

Metropolis–Hastings satisfies detailed balance for every target and every proposal

Theorem 9. The Metropolis–Hastings transition matrix satisfies detailed balance with π\piπ. So π\piπ is stationary (Lemma 8: balanced edges give πP=π\pi P=\piπP=π).
Proof. For x≠x′x\ne x'x=x′, move π(x)q(x′∣x)\pi(x)q(x'\mid x)π(x)q(x′∣x) inside the minimum:
π(x)P(x,x′)=π(x) q(x′∣x) min⁡{1,π(x′)q(x∣x′)π(x)q(x′∣x)}=min⁡{π(x)q(x′∣x), π(x′)q(x∣x′)}.\pi(x)P(x,x')=\pi(x)\,q(x'\mid x)\,\min\Big\{1,\frac{\pi(x')q(x\mid x')}{\pi(x)q(x'\mid x)}\Big\}=\min\big\{\pi(x)q(x'\mid x),\ \pi(x')q(x\mid x')\big\}.π(x)P(x,x′)=π(x)q(x′∣x)min{1,π(x)q(x′∣x)π(x′)q(x∣x′)​}=min{π(x)q(x′∣x), π(x′)q(x∣x′)}.

The right side does not change when xxx and x′x'x′ swap, so it also equals π(x′)P(x′,x)\pi(x')P(x',x)π(x′)P(x′,x). ■\blacksquare■

6 · Metropolis–Hastings · In today's machine learning

Speculative decoding: a small model drafts, the large model accepts or rejects

  • Problem: a large model ppp produces one token per slow, sequential pass. A small model qqq is fast but worse.
  • Idea: the small model proposes tokens; the large model checks several of them in one pass and accepts each with min⁡(1,p(x)/q(x))\min(1,p(x)/q(x))min(1,p(x)/q(x)): the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance for target ppp and proposal qqq.
  • After a rejection, a replacement is drawn from the leftover max⁡(0,p−q)\max(0,p-q)max(0,p−q), normalized. Next slide: why.
  • Benefit: most tokens come from the fast model, yet the output is exactly the large model's ppp: 2 to 3 times faster, same quality.

Y. Leviathan, M. Kalman, Y. Matias. Fast inference from transformers via speculative decoding. ICML 2023.

6 · Metropolis–Hastings · Limits

What Metropolis–Hastings does not solve

1. Rejections waste work. At 000 the walker stays 1936\tfrac{19}{36}3619​ of the time. Small moves are accepted but explore slowly; large moves explore fast but are mostly rejected.
2. Steps are correlated. Each step changes one variable, so NNN steps are worth fewer than NNN independent draws.
3. Barriers. An uphill move is accepted with e−ΔE/Te^{-\Delta E/T}e−ΔE/T, only 1243\tfrac1{243}2431​ at T=0.2T=0.2T=0.2: a cold walker stays in one peak for a long time.
4. No stopping rule. Convergence is guaranteed only as the number of steps grows; the chain never signals that it has arrived.

Next, Gibbs sampling removes the rejections. The end of today measures correlation, barriers and when to stop.

7 · Gibbs sampling · Idea, step by step

Redraw one variable from its conditional: only its factors are read

  • Pick a variable; hold all the others fixed.
  • Its two possible values have weights read from the factors that touch it, here 24 and 5.
  • Normalize over two values, not over 2n2^n2n states: 24+5=2924+5=2924+5=29.
  • Draw the new value with those probabilities. Nothing is ever rejected.
  • Two updates carried the walker from peak 100 to peak 111.

  • In general g(x)=∏afag(x)=\prod_af_ag(x)=∏a​fa​. A factor that does not contain xix_ixi​ is the same number above and below, so it cancels.
  • What remains are the factors touching xix_ixi​; their other variables form the Markov blanket of xix_ixi​.

On a grid: four neighbours, however large the grid.

Gibbs sampling is Metropolis–Hastings that always accepts

Definition (Gibbs sampler). Repeat: choose a variable iii (at random, or in turn); draw a new value xi∼p(xi∣x−i)x_i\sim p(x_i\mid x_{-i})xi​∼p(xi​∣x−i​), which reads only the factors containing xix_ixi​.

7 · Gibbs sampling · In today's machine learning

A masked language model redraws one token given all the others

  • A masked language model predicts pθ(xi∣x−i)p_\theta(x_i\mid x_{-i})pθ​(xi​∣x−i​) at any position; redrawing positions one by one is a Gibbs-style chain.
  • Our chain: all three conditionals come from one table ggg, so they fit together: Gibbs samples exactly ppp.
  • A masked model: each conditional is a separate network output. There may be no joint distribution with all of them, so the chain has no named target.
  • Fix: score whole sentences with one energy E(x)E(x)E(x); propose with the model's conditional; accept by Metropolis–Hastings. Target: e−E(x)/Ze^{-E(x)}/Ze−E(x)/Z.

8 · Mixing · Theorem

Both samplers converge geometrically, at the rate λ2\lambda_2λ2​

Theorem 11 (convergence rate). Let PPP on a finite set be irreducible, aperiodic, and satisfy detailed balance with π\piπ; let λ2<1\lambda_2\lt1λ2​<1 be its largest eigenvalue size other than 1. From every start x0x_0x0​, for every ttt:
∥Pt(x0,⋅)−π∥TV ≤ 121−π(x0)π(x0)  λ2 t.\big\|P^t(x_0,\cdot)-\pi\big\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\ \le\ \frac12\sqrt{\frac{1-\pi(x_0)}{\pi(x_0)}}\;\lambda_2^{\,t}.​Pt(x0​,⋅)−π​TV​ ≤ 21​π(x0​)1−π(x0​)​​λ2t​.
Metropolis–Hastings and random-scan Gibbs satisfy detailed balance, so it covers both samplers.
Proof idea. Detailed balance makes PPP symmetric after rescaling state xxx by π(x)\sqrt{\pi(x)}π(x)​: real eigenvalues, perpendicular eigenvectors. Split the start into π\piπ (eigenvalue 1) plus other parts; each step multiplies every other part by its eigenvalue, so they shrink at least like λ2t\lambda_2^tλ2t​. Cauchy–Schwarz converts this to total variation.
Our chain, start 010. 1277=4.39\tfrac12\sqrt{77}=4.3921​77​=4.39. Metropolis: 4.39×0.8004t4.39\times0.8004^t4.39×0.8004t; Gibbs: 4.39×0.8514t4.39\times0.8514^t4.39×0.8514t. The true distances lie far below: the bound gives the rate, not the constant.

P. Diaconis, D. Stroock. Geometric bounds for eigenvalues of Markov chains. Ann. Appl. Probab. 1(1), 36–61, 1991. Levin and Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, 2nd ed., 2017, Ch. 12.

8 · Mixing · Derivation

The waiting time grows exponentially in the height of the barrier over the temperature

  • From peak 100 (weight 24) to peak 111 (weight 20), the walker must pass a lighter state: 101 (weight 8) or 110 (weight 5). In energy E=−ln⁡gE=-\ln gE=−lng, a hill (top left).
  • The target is pT∝g1/Tp_T\propto g^{1/T}pT​∝g1/T, so Metropolis accepts 100 → 101 with
pT(101)pT(100)=(824)1/T=e−ln⁡3/T:\frac{p_T(101)}{p_T(100)}=\Big(\frac{8}{24}\Big)^{1/T}=e^{-\ln3/T}:pT​(100)pT​(101)​=(248​)1/T=e−ln3/T:

13\tfrac1331​ at T=1T=1T=1, but 1243\tfrac1{243}2431​ at T=0.2T=0.2T=0.2.

So the time to cross grows like eln⁡3/Te^{\ln3/T}eln3/T: each time 1/T1/T1/T grows by 1, the waiting time multiplies by about 3.

8 · Mixing · Check

On our chain: each step down in temperature makes mixing about three times slower

  • For each temperature, the relaxation time trel=1/(1−λ2)t_{\mathrm{rel}}=1/(1-\lambda_2)trel​=1/(1−λ2​), computed exactly from PPP: the steps the chain needs to forget its start.
  • 1/T=1,2,3,4,51/T=1,2,3,4,51/T=1,2,3,4,5: 5, 16, 47, 135, 378 steps. Each is about 3 times the one before (16/5=3.216/5=3.216/5=3.2, 378/135=2.8378/135=2.8378/135=2.8).
  • How to read the plot: across, 1/T1/T1/T; up, the relaxation time on a log scale (each gridline 10 times the one below). A constant factor per step, here about 3, shows as a straight line.
8 · Mixing · Idea, animated

Two chains, two different answers: the warning sign of poor mixing

  • 32×3232\times3232×32 grid, h=0h=0h=0: by symmetry the exact mean spin (the average of the 1,024 spins) is 0.
  • T=1.5T=1.5T=1.5, below the critical temperature Tc=2.269T_c=2.269Tc​=2.269, where the grid has two modes (mostly +1+1+1 or mostly −1-1−1): chain A says +0.99+0.99+0.99, chain B −0.99-0.99−0.99. Both confident, both wrong.
  • T=3T=3T=3: both fluctuate around 0 and agree.
One chain at T=1.5T=1.5T=1.5, 10,000 sweeps, a smooth trace. Trust its mean?
Answer. No: a stuck chain looks exactly like that. Only chains from different starts reveal it.
8 · Mixing · Idea

A walker repeats itself, so its steps carry less information than independent draws

  • We estimate P(X2=0)=0.6154P(X_2=0)=0.6154P(X2​=0)=0.6154 by averaging the score g=1g=1g=1 if x2=0x_2=0x2​=0, else 0.
  • Top: independent draws, as in Monte Carlo: the score switches often.
  • Bottom: one Metropolis walker. The score comes in long runs: a step changes one variable, or none.
  • The walker is already at ppp; the question is how accurate its average is. A run of equal scores is nearly one piece of evidence, repeated: on our chain, the walker's 60 scores give about the accuracy of 8 independent draws (the next slides compute this).
8 · Mixing · Definition

How accurate is an average along the walk? Its effective sample size

Definition. Lag kkk: the gap between steps ttt and t+kt+kt+k. Autocorrelation ρk=Corr⁡(g(Xt),g(Xt+k))\rho_k=\operatorname{Corr}\big(g(X_t),g(X_{t+k})\big)ρk​=Corr(g(Xt​),g(Xt+k​)): how alike the score is kkk steps apart (0: no memory; 1: identical). Left: our walker at ppp.

Independent draws: Var⁡(μ^N)=σ2/N\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_N)=\sigma^2/NVar(μ^​N​)=σ2/N, since variances add. Along the walk, the covariances add too:

Var⁡(μ^N)=σ2N2∑s,t=1Nρ∣s−t∣≈σ2N τ,τ=1+2∑k≥1ρk.\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_N)&=\frac{\sigma^2}{N^2}\sum_{s,t=1}^N\rho_{|s-t|}\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\,\tau,\qquad\tau=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k.\end{aligned}Var(μ^​N​)​=N2σ2​s,t=1∑N​ρ∣s−t∣​≈Nσ2​τ,τ=1+2k≥1∑​ρk​.​
  • τ\tauτ: how many walker steps are worth one independent draw. So NNN steps count as Neff=N/τN_{\mathrm{eff}}=N/\tauNeff​=N/τ, the effective sample size, and the error is σ/Neff\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}σ/Neff​​.
  • Independent draws: every ρk=0\rho_k=0ρk​=0, τ=1\tau=1τ=1. A stuck walker: τ\tauτ huge, NeffN_{\mathrm{eff}}Neff​ tiny.

g=1[x2=0]g=\mathbb 1[x_2=0]g=1[x2​=0] along the Metropolis chain at T=1T=1T=1, computed exactly from PPP:

ρ1=0.675,ρ2=0.508,ρ3=0.396, …τ=1+2∑k≥1ρk=7.29.\rho_1=0.675,\quad\rho_2=0.508,\quad\rho_3=0.396,\ \dots\qquad\tau=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k=7.29.ρ1​=0.675,ρ2​=0.508,ρ3​=0.396, …τ=1+2k≥1∑​ρk​=7.29.
Neff=10,0007.29=1,372,error=0.48651372=0.0131instead of 0.486510,000=0.0049.N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{10{,}000}{7.29}=1{,}372,\qquad\text{error}=\frac{0.4865}{\sqrt{1372}}=0.0131\quad\text{instead of }\frac{0.4865}{\sqrt{10{,}000}}=0.0049.Neff​=7.2910,000​=1,372,error=1372​0.4865​=0.0131instead of 10,000​0.4865​=0.0049.

8 · Mixing · Practice

Four checks before trusting a Markov chain average

CheckWhat to doWarning signSeen today
1. Burn-inleave the first steps out of the averageearly steps still sit near the startwalkers started at 010 came within 0.01 of ppp only after 7 steps
2. Trace plotplot the score g(Xt)g(X_t)g(Xt​) against tttlong flat stretchesthe walker at T=0.2T=0.2T=0.2 stays in one peak
3. Several chainsstart them far apart and comparethe chains disagreegrid at T=1.5T=1.5T=1.5: +0.99+0.99+0.99 against −0.99-0.99−0.99
4. Effective sample sizeestimate τ\tauτ; report σ/Neff\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}σ/Neff​​NeffN_{\mathrm{eff}}Neff​ tiny10,000 steps worth 1,372 draws

Why burn-in: the start is our choice, not a draw from ppp (010 has p=178p=\tfrac1{78}p=781​), so the first steps over-represent it.

R^\hat RR^ puts check 3 into one number: how far apart the chains' averages are, compared with how much each chain varies on its own. Chains that agree give R^≈1\hat R\approx1R^≈1. The grid chains at T=1.5T=1.5T=1.5 average +0.99+0.99+0.99 and −0.99-0.99−0.99 while each barely moves: R^\hat RR^ far above 1.

A. Gelman, D. B. Rubin. Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science 7(4), 457–472, 1992.

8 · Mixing · Synthesis

Three kinds of chains, and how to tell them apart

kindexample from todaysymptomdoes running longer help?
invaliduneven proposal without Hastings' ratioconverges to the wrong π\piπ: P(X2=0)=0.150P(X_2{=}0)=0.150P(X2​=0)=0.150no
valid but slowchain at T=0.2T=0.2T=0.2; grid at T=1.5T=1.5T=1.5chains disagree; τ\tauτ hugeyes, eventually
well mixedchain at T=1T=1T=1relaxation 5 steps, τ=7.3\tau=7.3τ=7.3error σ/Neff\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}σ/Neff​​
  • Invalid chains are caught by checking detailed balance on a few edges, or by a model small enough to enumerate, like ours.
  • Slow chains are caught by several chains from spread-out starts.
8 · Mixing · Note

A perfect sampler reproduces the model, including the model's mistakes

  • A sampler reproduces whatever model it is given. Suppose a learned model had g(010)=4g(010)=4g(010)=4 instead of 1: its energy −ln⁡4-\ln4−ln4 is too low.
  • A perfect Metropolis walker then visits 010 with 481=0.049\tfrac4{81}=0.049814​=0.049 instead of 178=0.013\tfrac1{78}=0.013781​=0.013: almost 4 times too often. The chain is valid; the model is wrong.
  • A real case: learned energies for atoms came out too low on rare configurations, such as a missing atom (Deng et al., 2025); samplers then visit them too often.
  • A valid sampler and a valid model are separate questions: check the model against reference data.

B. Deng, Y. Choi, P. Zhong et al. Systematic softening in universal machine learning interatomic potentials. npj Computational Materials 11, 9, 2025.

8 · Mixing · In today's machine learning

Slow mixing between modes is why diffusion models add noise at many scales

  • Target (top): two bumps; the left one holds 80% of the probability.
  • Langevin dynamics: x←x+ε∇ln⁡p(x)+2ε ξx\leftarrow x+\varepsilon\nabla\ln p(x)+\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\,\xix←x+ε∇lnp(x)+2ε​ξ, ξ\xiξ standard normal: drift toward higher probability, plus noise. No ZZZ needed.
  • Plain: walkers start half on each side; each stays in its nearest bump, almost never crossing the gap. About half end on the left (bottom), not 0.8: our chain's trap at T=0.2T=0.2T=0.2.
  • Annealed: add heavy noise so the bumps merge, then lower it step by step: about 0.8 end on the left. Score-based diffusion models sample this way.

Y. Song, S. Ermon. Generative modeling by estimating gradients of the data distribution. NeurIPS 2019.

8 · Mixing · In today's machine learning

Correlated evaluation questions shrink the effective number of questions

  • Background: a benchmark score is an average of NNN 0/1 scores, and its error bar a(1−a)/N\sqrt{a(1-a)/N}a(1−a)/N​ assumes independent questions.
  • Many benchmarks ask several questions about one passage. A model that misreads the passage tends to miss them all: answers in a group move together, like consecutive walker steps.
  • Main idea: groups of mmm questions, with correlation ρ\rhoρ between two answers of a group, are worth Neff=N/(1+(m−1)ρ)N_{\mathrm{eff}}=N/(1+(m-1)\rho)Neff​=N/(1+(m−1)ρ) independent questions: Kish's design effect.
N=1000, m=10, ρ=0.3:Neff=10001+9×0.3=10003.7=270.N=1000,\ m=10,\ \rho=0.3:\qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{1000}{1+9\times0.3}=\frac{1000}{3.7}=270.N=1000, m=10, ρ=0.3:Neff​=1+9×0.31000​=3.71000​=270.

At accuracy 0.80 the standard error grows from 0.0126 to 0.0126×3.7=0.02430.0126\times\sqrt{3.7}=0.02430.0126×3.7​=0.0243: the 95% interval widens from ±2.5\pm2.5±2.5 to ±4.8\pm4.8±4.8 points. Same fix as for chains: compute the error from the effective sample size (clustered standard errors).

L. Kish. Survey Sampling. Wiley, 1965. E. Miller. Adding error bars to evals. arXiv:2411.00640, 2024.

Two ideas avoid ZZZ: replace sums by averages (Monte Carlo, with error bars) and use only ratios (the Markov chain samplers). Both return in every later week.

Research

Three research questions you can start this week with today's tools

1. Power sampling on a toy language model

Question. How many Metropolis–Hastings steps does pαp^\alphapα need as α\alphaα grows?

First experiment. Read our chain as a 3-token model. Compare token-level temperature with Metropolis–Hastings on pαp^\alphapα for α=1,2,4,8\alpha=1,2,4,8α=1,2,4,8; plot the distance to the exact target against steps.

Start from Karan and Du (2025).

2. Where is Gibbs sampling slowest?

Question. How does the autocorrelation time τ\tauτ of the mean spin depend on TTT and on the grid size LLL?

First experiment. Measure τ\tauτ for L=8,16,32L=8,16,32L=8,16,32 and TTT from 1.5 to 3.5. Locate the peak and compare it with Tc=2.269T_c=2.269Tc​=2.269.

Cluster moves fix it: U. Wolff, Collective Monte Carlo updating for spin systems, Phys. Rev. Lett. 62(4), 361–364, 1989.

3. Is my sampler valid?

Question. When conditionals are learned separately, is there a joint distribution behind them?

First experiment. Perturb one entry inside the conditional of X2X_2X2​ only. Test detailed balance edge by edge; find the stationary distribution; repair it with a Metropolis–Hastings step.

Start from Goyal, Dyer and Berg-Kirkpatrick (2022).

Check yourself

Three questions to answer before Lecture 5

1. Symmetric proposal, g(x′)=3 g(x)g(x')=3\,g(x)g(x′)=3g(x). Acceptance of the move, and of the reverse move?
Answer. 1 and min⁡(1,13)=13\min(1,\tfrac13)=\tfrac13min(1,31​)=31​: ratio 3 on the edge, detailed balance.
2. A Markov chain runs four times longer. Its error?
Answer. Halved: error σ/N/τ\sigma/\sqrt{N/\tau}σ/N/τ​. A stuck chain can have τ\tauτ longer than any run.
3. 70% of proposals accepted, but the chain never leaves its peak. Reliable?
Answer. No. Acceptance measures local moves, not travel between peaks.
